title: Spotting False Information
tagline: How to check if news and messages are true before you share.
description: False messages spread fast on WhatsApp and Facebook, sometimes faster than the truth. They can cause fear, cost money and even put lives at risk. This course gives you simple habits to check a message, a photo or a video before you believe it or pass it on.
outcomes: Explain what false information is and why it spreads
Ask three questions before you share
Check who really sent a message
Spot edited photos and old videos
Find trusted sources of news in Zambia
Talk to others kindly about false news

modules.title: Why false information spreads
modules.summary: What it is, why we share it, and three questions to stop it.

lessons.title: What is false information?
lessons.body:
**False information** is anything that is presented as true but is not. It can be a message, a photo, a video, a voice note or a news story.

## Two kinds
- **Misinformation** is false, but the person sharing it believes it is true. Most people who forward false messages are trying to help.
- **Disinformation** is false on purpose. Someone made it to trick people, to make money, or to make people angry with a group or a leader.

Both do harm once they spread.

## What it can look like
- A message saying a drink cures a disease.
- A "warning" about a kidnapper in your area that never happened.
- A photo from another country, shared as if it happened in Zambia.
- A fake announcement of free money, jobs or bursaries from the government.
- A quote that a public figure never said.

## Why it matters
False health advice can stop people from getting real treatment. False alarms can cause panic and attacks on innocent people. Fake offers can trick people out of their money. And when false stories are everywhere, people stop trusting real information when it matters most.

## The good news
You do not need to be an expert. A few simple checks catch most false messages. And every time you stop a false message, you protect everyone in your groups.
key_points: Misinformation is shared by mistake; disinformation is shared on purpose
False messages can harm health, safety and money
Simple checks catch most false messages
lessons.try_it: Think of one message you saw this month that might not be true.

lessons.title: Why we share without checking
lessons.body:
False messages are designed to make us share them quickly. Knowing the tricks helps you slow down.

## Strong feelings
Messages that make us **afraid, angry or excited** spread the fastest. When we feel strongly, we want to act straight away, and we forget to check. If a message makes your heart beat faster, that is a sign to pause.

## "Forward to everyone you love"
Many false messages tell you to share them: *"Send this to 10 groups"*, *"Before they delete it"*. Real news does not need you to forward it.

## Trust in the sender
We believe messages from family, friends and church groups. But they usually forwarded it from someone else. A message from your aunt is only as true as its first source, which she probably does not know either.

## It fits what we already think
We believe stories that agree with what we already feel about a person or a group. Be extra careful with those.

## Wanting to be first
We like to be the one who shares news first. But being first and wrong helps no one.

## Slow down
Before you share, take a breath. Ask: *Do I really know this is true?* If not, it can wait. The message will still be there after you check.
key_points: Strong feelings are a sign to pause
Real news does not ask you to forward it
A trusted sender may still forward false news
lessons.try_it: The next time a message makes you angry or afraid, wait one hour before sharing it.

lessons.title: Three questions before you share
lessons.body:
Before you forward any message, ask these three questions. They take less than a minute.

## 1. Who made this?
Is there a name of a real person or organisation? Can you find it? *"A doctor at UTH says"* with no name is not a source. *"Forwarded many times"* means nobody knows where it started.

## 2. Where is the proof?
Does the message link to an official page or a known news outlet? Can you find the same story on the radio, ZNBC, a newspaper, or the official page of the ministry or company it mentions? If only WhatsApp groups are talking about it, be careful.

## 3. Does it make sense?
- Is it too good to be true, like free money for everyone?
- Is the date clear and recent?
- Are there many spelling mistakes, or a strange website address?
- Does it ask you to pay or share personal details?

## If you are not sure, do not share
Sharing a false message, even with good intentions, helps it spread. If you cannot answer the three questions, the safest choice is to **not forward it**.

You can still ask in the group: *"Does anyone know where this comes from?"* That helps others stop and think too.
key_points: Who made this?
Where is the proof?
Does it make sense?
lessons.try_it: Pick one forwarded message on your phone and ask the three questions about it.

quiz.explanation: Strong feelings and pressure to share are signs to slow down.

quiz.explanation: If you cannot check it, it can wait.

lessons.title: Checking who really sent it
lessons.body:
Scammers and liars often pretend to be someone important: a ministry, a bank, a hospital or a well-known person. Here is how to check.

## Forwarded labels
On WhatsApp, a message marked **Forwarded** or **Forwarded many times** did not start with the person who sent it to you. The double arrow means it has passed through many chats. Treat it with care.

## Fake screenshots
A **screenshot** is a picture of a screen. It is very easy to fake. Anyone can make a screenshot that looks like a news website or a government letter. If you see a screenshot of an announcement, look for the real announcement on the official page.

## Fake pages and accounts
On Facebook, fake pages copy the name and logo of real organisations. Check:

- Is there a **blue tick** next to the name? Many official pages have one.
- How long has the page existed, and how many followers does it have?
- Does it post normal content, or only offers and links?

## Official letters
Fake government letters circulate on WhatsApp. Real ones are usually also posted on the official website or Facebook page of the ministry. If you cannot find it there, do not trust it.

## Voice notes
Voice notes claiming to be from a doctor, a pastor or a leader are hard to check. Ask: who is this person? Can I find them? Without a name and a way to check, treat it as a rumour.
key_points: 'Forwarded many times' means the source is unknown
Screenshots are easy to fake
Check announcements on the official page
lessons.try_it: Look at the next forwarded message you receive and see if it has the forwarded label.

lessons.title: Old photos, new stories
lessons.body:
One of the most common tricks is to take a real photo or video and tell a **false story** about it. The picture is real, but it is from another place or another year.

For example, a photo of a flood in another country is shared as *"Lusaka this morning"*. Or a video of a protest from years ago is shared as if it is happening today.

## Signs a photo may be old or edited
- The buildings, cars, signs or language do not look like the place in the story.
- The weather or season does not match.
- People's clothes, car number plates or shop signs are from somewhere else.
- Parts of the picture look blurry, stretched or oddly cut.

## Search for the picture
You can check where a photo came from using **Google Lens**:

1. Save the photo to your phone.
2. Open the Google app or Google Photos, and tap the **Lens** icon (a small camera).
3. Choose the photo.
4. Tap **Find image source**, or scroll down to see where else it appears online.

If the same photo appears in a story from years ago or another country, the new story is false.

## Edited and fake videos
Videos can be cut to change their meaning, and computer programs can now make fake voices and faces. If a video shows a leader saying something shocking, check if trusted news outlets report it.
key_points: Real photos are often given false stories
Look for signs the place or time does not match
Use Google Lens to find where a photo first appeared
lessons.try_it: Use Google Lens on any photo in your gallery to see how it works.

lessons.title: Practice: check a message
lessons.body:
Let us practise with a message like the ones that go around WhatsApp.

*"URGENT!!! The Ministry of Health has announced that drinking hot water with lemon every 2 hours kills the virus. Hospitals don't want you to know this. Forward to all your groups to save lives!!!"*

## Step 1: How does it make you feel?
Worried, and eager to help your family. That strong feeling is the first warning sign.

## Step 2: Who made this?
It mentions the Ministry of Health, but gives no link, no date and no name. It says *hospitals don't want you to know*, which is a common trick to make you distrust real experts.

## Step 3: Where is the proof?
Look at the **Ministry of Health's official Facebook page** or website. Is this announcement there? Listen to the news. In this case, you would not find it.

## Step 4: Does it make sense?
A simple home cure that hospitals hide? Lots of exclamation marks? A demand to forward it everywhere? These are all red flags.

## The decision
**Do not forward it.** You can reply kindly in the group: *"I checked the Ministry of Health page and could not find this. Let us wait for the official advice."*

## Health messages need extra care
False health advice can stop people from going to a clinic. For health questions, always check with a health worker or the Ministry of Health.
key_points: Notice your feelings first
Check the official page of the organisation named
Reply kindly when you find a false message
lessons.try_it: Find one health message in your groups and check it against the Ministry of Health's official page.

lessons.body: A few short questions on this module. There is no time limit, and you can try again.

quiz.question: A WhatsApp message is marked 'Forwarded many times'. What does that tell you?
options: It has passed through many chats and the source is unknown
quiz.explanation: The label means the message started somewhere else, often unknown.

quiz.question: You see a screenshot of a 'government announcement'. What is the best check?
options: Trust it because it looks official
Look for it on the ministry's official page
quiz.explanation: Screenshots are easy to fake. The official page is the real source.

options: It is an old or foreign photo with a false story
quiz.explanation: Details that do not match the place are a strong sign of a false story.

quiz.explanation: Google Lens searches for other copies of the same image.

modules.title: Trusted sources and talking kindly
modules.summary: Where to check, and how to correct others without a fight.

lessons.title: Finding trusted sources in Zambia
lessons.body:
Checking a message is easier when you know where reliable information comes from.

## Signs of a trustworthy source
- It has a **name** and is easy to contact.
- It says **who** said something and **when**.
- It corrects its mistakes openly.
- Other trusted sources report the same thing.

## Places to check in Zambia
- **National and community radio and TV**, such as ZNBC news and local stations.
- **Established newspapers**, in print or on their official websites.
- The **official websites and verified Facebook pages** of ministries, councils and public bodies. For example, health news from the Ministry of Health, and election information from the **Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)**.
- For money and banking warnings: the **Bank of Zambia** and your bank or network's official pages.

## Two sources are better than one
If you can find the same story in **two trusted places**, it is much more likely to be true. If only one unknown page or a WhatsApp group is saying it, wait.

## Be careful with these
- Pages with no clear owner, or new pages with very few posts.
- Headlines in capital letters with *SHOCKING* or *BREAKING* and no details.
- Websites with names that copy real outlets but with small changes.

## Opinions are not news
A post sharing someone's opinion, even a famous person's, is not the same as a news report. Both can be useful, but know which one you are reading.
key_points: Trusted sources give names and dates
Check official pages for announcements
Look for the same story in two trusted places
lessons.try_it: Follow the official page of one ministry or public body you care about.

lessons.title: Talking to others kindly about false news
lessons.body:
When you find a false message in a family or church group, it is tempting to say *"This is fake, how can you believe this?"* But that often makes people defensive, and they stop listening.

## Correct the message, not the person
Most people share false messages because they care. Start with that.

*"Thank you for looking out for us. I checked the Ministry of Health page and I could not find this. Here is what they say instead."*

## Give the true information
Do not just say something is false. Share what is true, with a link or source. People are more likely to accept a correction when they get something useful in return.

## Keep it short and calm
One clear, friendly reply is better than a long argument. Avoid capital letters and many exclamation marks.

## Talk in private if needed
If someone might feel embarrassed in front of the group, send them a private message instead.

## It is fine to say "I don't know"
Sometimes you cannot prove a message is true or false. You can say: *"I am not sure this is true. Let us wait for official news before we share it."* That alone stops it spreading.

## Lead by example
When you make a mistake and share something false, say so in the group. It shows others that checking is normal, and it builds trust.
key_points: Correct the message, not the person
Share the true information with a source
It is fine to say 'let us wait for official news'
lessons.try_it: Write a kind reply you could use the next time someone shares a false message.

lessons.title: Rumours at important times
lessons.body:
False information spreads most during **elections**, **disease outbreaks** and **disasters**. At these times, rumours can cause real harm.

## During elections
- Be careful of messages about voting dates, places or rules. Check them with the **Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)** official page.
- Fake results and fake quotes from candidates often appear. Wait for official announcements.
- Messages that make you hate another group or tribe are often designed to divide people. Do not share them.

## During outbreaks
- Get health advice from the **Ministry of Health**, clinics and health workers.
- Be very careful of home cures, and claims that medicines or vaccines are dangerous, from unknown sources.

## During disasters
- During floods or fires, false messages about danger or help can send people to the wrong place.
- Follow official instructions from the **Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit**, your local council and the police, on radio and their official pages.

## Your role
At these times, people in your groups may listen to you. Share only checked information, point people to official sources, and do not forward rumours, even to ask if they are true. A calm voice in a group can stop panic.
key_points: Rumours spread most during elections, outbreaks and disasters
Check election information with the ECZ
Point people to official sources
lessons.try_it: Find and save the official page of the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

lessons.title: Final check: Spotting false information
lessons.body: Questions covering the whole course. Score 70% or more to complete it. You can try again as many times as you like.

quiz.question: What are the three questions to ask before you share?
options: Who made this? Where is the proof? Does it make sense?
Is it long? Is it funny? Is it new?
Who sent it? What time is it? Is it a video?
Is it free? Is it urgent? Is it in English?
quiz.explanation: These three questions catch most false messages.

quiz.question: Where should you check information about voting dates and places?
options: The Electoral Commission of Zambia's official page
A Facebook page with no owner
quiz.explanation: The ECZ is the official source for election information.

quiz.question: Your uncle shares a false health message in the family group. What is the best reply?
options: A kind reply with the correct information and its source
quiz.explanation: Correct the message, not the person, and share what is true.

quiz.question: A story appears on one unknown page only. What should you do?
options: Wait until a trusted source reports it
quiz.explanation: Two trusted sources are better than one unknown page.

quiz.question: A video shows a leader saying something shocking. What is a good check?
options: Believe it, videos cannot be faked
See whether trusted news outlets report it
quiz.explanation: Videos can be cut or faked. Trusted outlets help you check.
